newsitem.title: USA: U.S. base metals markets quiet but steady.
newsitem.headline: U.S. base metals markets quiet but steady.

text.p: Although physical base metals spot trading is fairly quiet in the United States, premiums are holding steady for the rest of the year and into 1997, traders said.
Aluminum consumers are opting to buy only what they need to avoid piling up inventory before the year end, traders added.
Premiums were quoted at 4.25 to 4.50 cents per pound over LME cash for the rest of 1996, but with some parcels of business concluded over 5 cents for very prompt delivery.
"It's not a normal market in November and December. When people run out, they will pay anything to get it in," a dealer said.
Premiums on 1997 business were quoted at 4.00 to 4.25 cents.
"When copper went down earlier this week, aluminum held its own which I thought created a bit of a base," a producer official said.

Zinc premiums, and particularly the LME price remain relatively firm as rumors abound that leading finacier George Soros has put money in the market. Soros' spokesman in New York was not available for comment.
Metals industry consultant David Cook of Lake Engineering said whatever lay behind the talk, people were beginning to take an interest again in zinc for good fundamental reasons.
"They are realising it's a good metal for the next year and a half and prices are going to go up considerably," Cook said.
Premiums on zinc were quoted at 5.25 to 6.00 cents per pound over LME cash.

"Premiums will probably come off a little bit as we get more tonnage over here, attracted by the high premiums," Cook said. "There will also be tonnage coming in anticipation of the closing of the St Lawrence seaway and the Greak Lakes for the winter. You always get a little stocking."

A zinc producer official said there was no reason for prices to go down. "But if this General Motors strike continues, that is one threat to future consumption if it's going to last too long," he added.
North American lead producer said the market was "running along fairly steadily".
Lead premiums were quoted at 3 to 4 cents per pound over LME cash.
Some observers were waiting for the European battery season to begin kicking in within a month to boost demand enough to pull metal out of the LME's Helsinborg warehouse and help push prices up.
